headline_marked: [[Meta AI director launches Ndoc]] to replace Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
headline: Meta AI director launches Ndoc to replace Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
summary: Rohit Patel, former Meta Superintelligence Labs director, has unveiled Ndoc, an AI-native startup designed to unify fragmented workflows and replace traditional office suites with a single, verifiable workspace.
details: After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company to launch Ndoc. This new startup is pitched as an AI-native replacement for the Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.

Patel designed Ndoc to go beyond layering AI onto existing workflows. Its goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and "ChatGPT copy-paste" with one unified workspace.

This workspace allows all colleagues to access documents, even if they are not signed up for Ndoc. The platform brings three components together: The Stage tab for presentations and dashboards, the Narrative tab for analyses and generated figures, and the Model tab for underlying datasets and Python scripts.

Patel's background in reinforcement learning and evaluating AI trustworthiness influenced Ndoc's design. He believes users should be able to check AI's work, allowing them to find and verify the Python scripts used to create documents.

Users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. The platform also maintains memory across the user, the specific document, their team, and the company.
Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open-source models. Patel states this approach makes it considerably less expensive to run compared to alternatives built on frontier AI models.
Patel's larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. Documents can be exported as a single ".ndoc.html" file, openable in any browser, a format he plans to open source.

This open-source vision was a key reason for his departure from Meta, allowing him to move quickly without the bureaucratic hurdles of a large company. He aims to enable other developers to build apps compatible with Ndoc's format, avoiding vendor lock-in.

Ndoc faces significant competition from major AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, which are also developing enterprise AI tools. These competitors often integrate their AI models directly into existing platforms like Google Workspace and Microsoft 365.

Patel acknowledges the competition but argues that most AI labs have the wrong idea, merely attaching AI to spreadsheets. He believes Ndoc's ground-up, AI-native approach is a fundamental shift, akin to using a tractor instead of putting lights on bulls for tilling.

headline_marked: [[Ford Fathom EV starts at $28,350]] with new low-cost home backup power chargers
headline: Ford Fathom EV starts at $28,350 with new low-cost home backup power chargers
summary: The new Home Power Station and Home Backup Power packages are up to 60% cheaper than previous generations, making vehicle-to-home power more accessible. The Fathom can deliver over 10 kW to a home, acting as a small standby generator.
details: Ford announced two new EV chargers for its forthcoming Fathom pickup, enabling it to power homes or the grid. The Fathom itself will start at $28,350, making it an affordable option for vehicle-to-home capabilities.

These new chargers are about half the cost of Ford's existing products, significantly lowering the barrier to entry for V2X services. The Fathom can deliver over 10 kW to a home, enough to power essential appliances like a refrigerator and air conditioner for about half a day.

The Home Power Station, priced around $650, allows users to charge the Fathom during low power prices and send electricity back to the home when prices are high, helping to reduce utility bills. This device is 50% cheaper than Ford's first-gen bidirectional charger.

The Home Backup Power package, costing around $2,100, bundles the Home Power Station with a Home Backup Panel. This enables the Fathom to power parts or all of a home during outages, representing a 60% cost reduction from the previous generation.
Installation costs are separate and can be substantial, potentially up to $10,000 depending on electrical work needed. Ford plans to release more details on installer partnerships later.

Both chargers allow Fathom customers to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs). Owners can sell electricity back to the grid, potentially earning upwards of $1,000 per year, helping utilities manage growing grid demands.
